notes.33r.299: Line 300 holds only the decorated initial A of Apres, which the transcription sets on a line of its own; 'Afterwards' is given there. Line 301: le clerc is taken as the subject despite its oblique form, as the case system breaks down in this manuscript, with l' as the pupil. Line 306: Romanie, the Roman (Byzantine) empire or the Romance-speaking lands. Line 327: le mist, 'set him (or it) to necromancy'; subject and object unclear. Line 328: 'of the six', though line 325 speaks of seven arts. Line 345: the plural 'they' is as written. Line 348: adesens read as a de sens.

nodes.text: how many they are in their company.
Afterwards
the clerk taught him astrology.
This is an art that is much coveted;
whoever knew it, his life would greatly please him,
and he would have honour and wealth,
and great possessions and very great lordship.
He would know well how things go in Romania,
and what is done over there in heathen lands,
or over here in France the well-provided,
or anywhere in the whole world that turns.
By this art Joseph was wholly lord
over Pharaoh and over his company.
Whoever knows this art, I will not lie to you,
knows very well what is to come.
If he saw two champions come
who were to fight in a field,
he would know well which of them was to win.
The senators of Rome, without a lie,
took counsel by this art in former days
about hard battles and heavy fights;
they would know full well who would get the worst of it.
By this art, I assure you, there knew
all the three kings that Jesus Christ was born,
and they sought him out from foreign lands,
and also by the star that appeared.
Of these seven arts that I am describing to you
he read in a book, every one, I assure you;
at the last he set him to necromancy.
That is an art, the most hated of the six,
for the devil is wholly master of it.
Whoever learns this art, I assure you,
is not much hated by the devil.
By this art one knows of the thefts
that thieves commit, both by night and by day,
and from it one knows the barking of the mastiffs.
There is no bird in the world, however small,
nor however great, marvellous or stout,
whose speech and sayings he would not know.
He can well make a partridge of himself,
or a goshawk, a falcon or a merlin;
of two wisps of straw he makes two strong packhorses.
He could never be put in so strong a prison
that he would not get out of it before it was midday.
He would have taken those inside in a single day
and destroyed and burned the whole country,
and if they wished they would take them all alive;
not a single one of them would be harmed,
nor would there be any fighting or strife.

“may it please God, the king of paradise,
